issues.item: Triggers: Victim Similarity: People who look similar to the victims
issues.explanation: For a single-patient assault trauma, 'people who look similar to the victims' is clinically incoherent because it implies multiple victims or identification with other victims rather than the patient's own assault experience. A more self-referential trigger would be expected.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening
issues.explanation: 'Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening' sits awkwardly with the rest of the profile's self-directed shame and identity-change appraisals. It implies confidence that another person would have prevented the assault, which conflicts with the patient's own vulnerability/self-blame framing in a way that is hard to integrate clinically.

issues.item: Triggers: Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
issues.explanation: For an assault trauma in a 70-year-old male, 'medical procedures' plus 'body shame' implies a strong bodily injury/medical aftermath theme, but the rest of the profile does not support that theme. With only offender cues and intrusive thoughts otherwise present, the medical trigger looks insufficiently anchored and may be mismatched to the rest of the assault profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: 'Body shame' is not impossible after assault, but alongside 'defective self' and 'unrecognisable self' it suggests a bodily violation/injury-focused appraisal pattern that is not well reflected in the other selected nodes. The triggers and strategies mainly reflect avoidance, numbing, and offender-related activation rather than body-focused trauma processing.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Catastrophising Others: I worry obsessively about bad things happening to people I care about
issues.explanation: 'Catastrophising others' is weakly connected to the rest of the selected profile. The active formulation links Triggers strongly with Maladaptive Strategies and Negative Appraisals strongly with Triggers, but this strategy is not a plausible direct response to the chosen triggers (medical procedures, intrusive thoughts, offender cues) and is not well explained by the selected appraisals. It addresses a generalized harm concern that is otherwise absent from the profile.

vignette:
Richard is a 70-year-old married salesman who came to treatment months after being assaulted in a strip mall parking lot he had used for years between client visits. He had stopped after work to pick up takeout and was walking back to his car when a man who was visibly drunk approached him, first asking for money and then turning aggressive when Richard hesitated. What stayed with him was not only the shove and the blows, but the smell on the man's breath when he got close enough to curse at him-stale alcohol, heavy and sour-and the sudden, humiliating sense of being overpowered in a place that had once felt ordinary. Richard remembered seeing the man's face at close range as he tried to shield himself, and that image had remained fixed in a way that felt more vivid than the rest of the evening.

In the weeks afterward, Richard found that the assault kept forcing its way back into his mind. Unwanted thoughts would break into his day without warning, especially if he caught the smell of alcohol on a customer, passed someone on the sidewalk who resembled the attacker, or thought he had seen the same man again near that shopping center. Even when he knew he could not be certain it was the offender, the jolt in his body was immediate. Those moments did not stay confined to the moment itself; they changed how he moved through his days. Because the parking lot where it happened had become intolerable to approach, he began reorganizing his sales routes to avoid that entire area. If a client meeting would take him nearby, he found reasons to reschedule or asked a coworker to cover it. When unwanted thoughts pushed in, he tried to clamp down on them and force his mind elsewhere, and when that did not work he would go emotionally flat, telling himself there was no point feeling anything at all if it only made him vulnerable again.

These same moments also cut directly into the way Richard had come to see himself. Each time he smelled alcohol and was thrown back to the assault, or each time he caught sight of a man he feared might be the offender, he was flooded not only with fear but with a harsh, familiar conclusion: that the event happened because of how he handled himself. He had come to believe he should have walked away faster, spoken differently, seen the danger sooner. In his mind, the fact that he had been caught off guard said something shameful about him. He described feeling that there was something wrong with him as a person, and that the man he had become since the assault was unrecognizable to him-more guarded, smaller, less certain. The triggers did not just remind him of what happened; they seemed to confirm his worst view of himself every time they appeared.

Over time, those beliefs made the intrusions more potent rather than less. Because Richard was so preoccupied with the idea that he had failed in some essential way, his mind kept returning to the attacker's face and the moments just before the first shove, searching for the exact point at which he had "caused" things to go wrong. Seeing someone who resembled the offender could start a long spiral of mental replay. A whiff of alcohol in a restaurant during a sales lunch could pull him into the same self-accusing loop, leaving him distracted and tense through the rest of the meeting. What frightened him most was not only that the memories came back, but that they seemed to prove he was no longer himself. The more defective he felt, the more easily his attention snagged on cues of danger and on the assault itself.

This pattern had begun to constrict his life. His work had always depended on ease with strangers and comfort moving from place to place, yet now he planned routes around avoidance rather than efficiency, and his sales numbers had slipped. At home, his wife could feel the distance in him. Richard did not want to talk about the assault because he was trying so hard not to think about it, and he often sat through evenings dulled out and unreachable. He finally sought help after realizing he had turned down another longstanding client simply because the office was near the parking lot where he had been attacked. What brought him in was a mixture of shame and alarm: shame that he believed he had let one incident remake him, and alarm that the smell of alcohol, the glimpse of a familiar-looking man, or an unwanted thought could still strip away the life he had known. What he hopes for now is to feel recognizable to himself again; what he fears is that this diminished version of him is permanent.
